narrative:
The model predicted a 63.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) in your third year, compared to an average of nearly 6 among accepted students, signaled to the model that you struggled to perform at the level typically needed to pass the bar.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and worked in the opposite direction. At 36, it is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, so it provided a modest pull toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the negative signal from your class rank.

Your first-year class ranking came third in importance and again pushed the outcome toward failure. Ranking in the second decile, well below the average of 6 among accepted students, reinforced the pattern of academic performance that the model associates with higher risk of not passing the bar.

Taken together, these academic indicators outweighed your solid family income, full-time study plans, and respectable undergraduate GPA. To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record, consider retaking the LSAT if you can raise it meaningfully, or explore schools and programs with different admissions models that weigh other strengths more heavily.
